notes.meaning: The Philistines carried the Ark of the Covenant away as a prize of war from the battlefield at Ebenezer to Ashdod, one of their five major cities. Even though Israel had lost the battle, the Ark remained God's holy chest. The Philistines thought they had captured Israel's God, but He was about to show them His mighty power.

The Philistines placed the Ark inside the temple of Dagon, their main god, right next to his statue. In the ancient world, conquerors put captured sacred objects before their idols to show their god had won the battle. Dagon was likely a god of grain and crops, though older traditions pictured him as half-man and half-fish.

Early the next morning, the people of Ashdod discovered Dagon lying face down on the ground in front of the Ark, like a servant bowing in worship. Instead of seeing that the God of Israel was greater than their idol, the Philistines thought the statue had fallen by accident. They simply picked Dagon up and set him back in his place.

The next morning, Dagon had fallen again before the Ark, but this time his head and both hands were broken off and lying at the doorway. In ancient warfare, victors cut off the head and hands of fallen enemies to show total conquest. Only the idol's trunk was left, proving that their god had no wisdom to guide them and no strength to defend them.

Because Dagon's broken pieces landed on the doorway, stepping on the threshold became strictly forbidden in his temple. Instead of giving up their broken idol and turning to the true God, the Philistines created a new superstitious ceremony to jump over the spot. This practice was remembered and observed for generations.

God turned His judgment from the lifeless stone idol to the bodies of the people living in Ashdod and nearby villages. A painful sickness broke out, ravaging the population with severe swellings. The Philistines quickly felt that the Lord was directly punishing them for their disrespect.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern commentators suggest the painful swellings were the buboes of bubonic plague, which is carried by rats and matches the mention of mice in the next chapter.

notes.meaning: The people of Ashdod realized right away that their suffering was not an accident or a natural illness. They openly admitted that the God of Israel was striking both them and their god Dagon. Yet instead of repenting and asking God for mercy, they only wanted to get His holy Ark far away from them.

Ashdod's leaders called a council of the rulers of the five Philistine cities to decide what to do with the Ark. The Philistines still loved their war trophy too much to give it back to Israel, so they agreed to move it inland to the city of Gath. They hoped that changing locations would make the plague stop.

Moving the Ark did not help, because God's judgment followed it directly to Gath. The Lord threw the city into wild panic and struck everyone with the outbreak of tumors, from young children to old men. Trying to run from God's presence only spread the misery and destruction further.

The rulers next sent the Ark to Ekron, another Philistine city a few miles north of Gath. News of the horror had traveled ahead, and the people of Ekron cried out in terror the moment it arrived. They accused their own leaders of bringing the Ark among them just to kill them and their families.

The terrified leaders of Ekron called another council of all the Philistine rulers, demanding that the Ark be sent back to Israel. Deadly panic had gripped the whole city because God's punishing hand was falling on them with crushing weight. They finally realized that keeping God's Ark in Philistine territory was costing them their lives.

Those who did not die immediately suffered intense agony from the tumors. The wailing and screams from the city were so loud that the outcry was said to reach heaven. Without an army or a single human weapon, God demonstrated His supreme glory over the enemies of His people.
